questions.q: What does trips.groupBy("VendorID") return, on its own?
options: A GroupedData object — not a DataFrame, and it can't be shown directly
A fully computed DataFrame ready to .show()
A Python dictionary of vendor IDs and their row counts
An error, since groupBy() requires an aggregation argument
questions.explain: It's a statement of intent — waiting for an aggregation like .count() to turn it into an actual DataFrame.

options: Because groupBy() alone returns GroupedData, which has no .show() method the way a DataFrame does
Because VendorID is spelled incorrectly in this example
Because groupBy() only works on numeric columns
It doesn't actually fail — this is valid, working code
questions.explain: Chaining .count() onto groupBy() is what turns it into an actual, showable DataFrame.

options: A count for every unique combination of VendorID and passenger_count
A single overall row count, ignoring both columns
The count of VendorID values only, ignoring passenger_count entirely
An error, since groupBy() only accepts one column
questions.explain: Each distinct combination of the grouped columns gets its own row and count in the result.

questions.q: How does PySpark's groupBy() compare to Pandas' groupby() from Lesson 26?
options: Same underlying concept and almost the same name — grouping rows that share a value
They are entirely unrelated concepts with different purposes
PySpark's groupBy() only works on string columns
Pandas' groupby() requires an aggregation immediately, unlike PySpark's
questions.explain: The PySpark version is intentionally incomplete on its own, needing an aggregation chained on.

questions.q: What's the simplest aggregation you can chain onto groupBy()?
options: .count() — how many rows landed in each group
.select() — choosing which columns to display
.filter() — removing rows that don't match a condition
.cast() — converting a column's data type
questions.explain: The next lesson's .agg() expands on this with sums, averages, and multiple statistics per group at once.
